newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Spiegel says Tietmeyer considers EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spiegel says Tietmeyer considers EMU delay.

text.p: Germany's Der Spiegel magazine said on Saturday that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has asked whether Germany and France can consider delaying the start of European monetary union (EMU) set for January 1, 1999.
"Wouldn't it be a possibility, together with France, to agree to a delay in the start of the euro?" the magazine quoted Tietmeyer as saying in an article to be published on Monday.
Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if Bonn and Paris did not meet the entry criteria this year.
The Maastricht Treaty has requirements on budget deficits and debts, interest rates, inflation and foreign exchange rates that must be met in 1997 to join currency union at the start.
A Spiegel spokesman said the magazine had not spoken directly with Tietmeyer, saying the information was based on talks with sources in Germany. He declined further comment.
A Bundesbank spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment on the Spiegel article.

Prospects for a delay rose have risen after Bonn and the Bundesbank openly clashed over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue the bank's reserves and demand a payout of the hidden profits to help Bonn cut its budget deficit.

The Bundesbank, a fierce advocate of fiscal austerity and opponent of tricks in meeting the criteria for monetary union, on Wednesday openly critcised Waigel's plan and said it could undermine the new currency, the euro, from the start.

German central bank sources have said in the past the question of delaying the union should not be made into a total taboo if either Germany or France, considered crucial members, failed to meet entry criteria in the treaty.
Tietmeyer has not made the case in the past for a delay in currency union but has simply asked the question as to whether this should be considered, bank sources have said.
Tietmeyer has not commented publically on the row since the bank issued a statement on Wednesday criticising Waigel's plan.
But he is expected to strongly oppose the plan in a meeting scheduled for next week with Bonn lawmakers in a closed-door meeting of parliament's finance committee.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government plans to introduce legislation next week to change Bundesbank laws and allow for the transfer despite the central bank's hefty objection.
Waigel has said his plan does not attack the Bundesbank's independence and that the bank agreed with him on the need to value the gold and currency reserves towards market prices.

He has said the bank's only point of contention was whether the reserves would be revalued in 1997, or in 1999 as the bank prefers. Waigel has also said Bonn does not need the Bundesbank funds to make it into EMU, a claim disputed by some economists.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen told Reuters on Friday the break with Germany's consensus-led tradition could lead to "disastrous" consequences if Bonn fails to back down from the plan.

The deputy secretary-general of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) added his voice to the debate on Saturday, saying Bonn's plan could hurt the country's credibility heading into EMU.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Kumiharu Shigehara said he was not sure why Germany wanted to implement the plan now, but the OECD would be watching its effects on Europe.
"All I can say at this stage is that credibility is crucial in all respects of the efforts towards monetary union," he said.
